publications.title: N8N LinkedIn Creators Agent: A Workflow for Discovering AI Builders at Scale
publications.subtitle: Zenodo
publications.description: A growing number of LinkedIn users share automation workflows and AI agent builds that demonstrate how everyday tasks can be simplified or eliminated. These posts often include screenshots, diagrams, or step-by-step explanations and serve as practical learning resources for builders and practitioners. However, discovering this content consistently is difficult. Manual feed browsing is inefficient, search results are noisy, and valuable posts are often buried beneath unrelated content. This paper presents a modular automation workflow built in n8n that supports the discovery of LinkedIn creators who publicly share workflow-based solutions. The system combines AI-assisted query generation, public Google search, structured result extraction, lightweight email pattern inference, and persistent logging. The project was developed over a period of more than three months with iterative feedback and collaboration involving both undergraduate and graduate students. Rather than acting as a ranking or recommendation system, the workflow functions as a repeatable discovery tool that reduces the time required to find creators whose workflows address common, time-consuming tasks. The results demonstrate that discovery itself can be treated as an automation problem and addressed using transparent, public, and modular systems.

publications.title: The Great Silence: An Experimental Exploration of the Fermi Paradox and Its Implications for Astrobiology
publications.subtitle: Zenodo
publications.description: The Fermi Paradox, encapsulated by the question "Where are they?", highlights the profound contradiction between the high probability of extraterrestrial intelligence existing in our vast universe and the complete absence of observational evidence for such civilizations. This paper delves into the historical context of the paradox, explores its quantitative underpinnings through the Drake Equation, and rigorously examines a spectrum of hypotheses proposed to resolve this perplexing silence. We categorize these solutions into those suggesting the rarity of intelligent life, those positing the undetectability or disinterest of advanced civilizations, and those related to our own temporal position in cosmic history. Furthermore, this paper discusses the experimental dimensions of the Fermi Paradox, outlining how ongoing and future scientific endeavors, including SETI, exoplanet research, and astrobiological studies, are actively engaged in testing these hypotheses. By synthesizing current knowledge and charting pathways for future inquiry, we aim to underscore the Fermi Paradox not merely as a philosophical quandary, but as a robust driver of empirical investigation into the fundamental questions of life's prevalence and destiny in the cosmos.

publications.title: Origami-Based Kinetic and Radiative Shielding for Space Habitats: A Computational and Theoretical Investigation into Deployable Yoshimura Structures
publications.subtitle: Zenodo
publications.description: The long-term human habitation of space is critically dependent on the development of lightweight, multifunctional, and deployable structures. Two of the most significant threats to crew and habitat integrity are hypervelocity impacts from micrometeoroids and orbital debris (MMOD) and the constant bombardment of galactic cosmic rays (GCR) and solar particle events (SPE). This paper presents an experimental investigation, conducted through computational simulation, into the feasibility of using an origami-based structure, specifically the Yoshimura crease pattern, as a dual-purpose shield. A Yoshimura cylinder was designed and subjected to Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to simulate its response to kinetic impacts. A separate theoretical model was developed to assess its capacity as a deployable container for radiation-shielding material. The results from the FEA simulations indicate that the Yoshimura pattern’s unique buckling mechanism effectively absorbs and distributes impact energy, reducing the risk of penetration. Furthermore, the volumetric expansion during deployment allows the structure to contain a significant mass of radiation-shielding material, increasing its areal density and protective capabilities. This research suggests that origami engineering, exemplified by the Yoshimura pattern, offers a viable and innovative solution for creating next-generation, adaptable shielding systems for future space habitats.

publications.title: Cryptocurrency and Financial Inclusion
publications.subtitle: Zenodo
publications.description: This paper examines how the adoption of Bitcoin has affected financial inclusion, banking access, and economic activity in El Salvador, with a particular focus on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in underbanked regions. After El Salvador became the first country to recognize Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, it created a unique opportunity to study how cryptocurrency functions outside of theory and within a real national economy. Using a mixed-methods approach, this research combines a review of academic literature, policy analysis, and media reporting with quantitative analysis of cryptocurrency market data and financial infrastructure indicators.The quantitative component includes correlation, regression, and predictive analysis of cryptocurrency price and transaction volume data, as well as an examination of Bitcoin ATM availability relative to population across major cities. These results are supported by qualitative findings that explore public adoption, SME experiences, and broader economic concerns such as volatility, infrastructure limitations, and financial stability. The findings suggest that while Bitcoin has expanded access to digital financial tools and introduced potential efficiencies in transactions, its impact on financial inclusion has been uneven, particularly in rural and underbanked areas. For SMEs, Bitcoin presents both opportunities and challenges, offering faster payments while also creating risks related to volatility, technical barriers, and implementation costs. Overall, this study highlights the mixed outcomes of cryptocurrency adoption in El Salvador and contributes to ongoing discussions about whether digital currencies can meaningfully support financial inclusion and economic development in developing economies.

projects.description: OceanGuard is an AI-powered platform that uses real-time CNN data to identify predict where heavy amounts of trash and debris will end up across the world, and automatically organizes clean ups to mitigate them as they happen. activity.title: A few days ago, SCU Product Club hosted our annual hackathon in partnership with Jolli AI - and honestly? The room's energy blew us away. Participants had just 2 hours to explore Jolli AI's connected knowledge platform and develop a go-to-market strategy to drive real user adoption. No code. Just creativity, strategy, and sharp thinking. And every single team delivered. 🙌 The pitches were thoughtful, bold, and genuinely impressive - from viral growth loops to developer community plays to product-led adoption strategies. Watching students think like founders in real time was exactly the energy we set out to create. Congratulations to our winning team: Raghav Gupta , Shikhar Sisodia , and Dhruv Vootkuri - who walked away with the $1,000 execution fund to bring their GTM strategy to life. We can't wait to see what you build. 🏆 A very special thank you to Nick Chong , CEO of Jolli AI and SCU MBA alumnus, for joining us virtually, presenting the challenge himself, and staying engaged through every single pitch. Really happy to share that our team won two awards at SF Hacks at SFSU 2026: Best Hack for Sustainability in Education and Major League Hacking Best Use of Solana. We built OceanGuard, an AI system that plans ocean cleanups on its own. You give it pollution data, and it figures out where to send crews, calls the site contacts, posts job listings, handles donations, the whole thing. Nobody has to sit there and organize it manually. For the education side, we made a scoreboard where schools can adopt cities and compete by doing actual cleanups, running classroom lessons, fundraising, that kind of stuff. The idea was to make sustainability something students can track and get competitive about, instead of just hearing about it in a lecture. For Solana , we built a donation system where people can fund specific cleanup supplies on-chain. Real transactions, real wallets, everything verifiable on Solana Explorer. We picked Solana because the fees are basically nothing, which matters when you're trying to get every dollar to the actual cleanup. Huge shoutout to Dhruv Vootkuri , Arya Cherukuri , and Ryan Saleh -- couldn't have pulled this off without this team. 48 hours well spent. #SFHacks2026 #OceanGuard #Hackathon #Solana #Sustainability ...more

At CruzHacks , our team was fortunate to receive two awards: Best Use of Solana (sponsored by Major League Hacking ) and Most Ambitious Project. In just 36 hours, we set out to explore how fully autonomous drone delivery could realistically operate within neighborhoods and college campuses—and turned that idea into a working system. From a technical standpoint, we focused heavily on autonomy and real-world feasibility. Using Microsoft AirSim with simulated LiDAR, GPS, and IMU data, we applied physics-based modeling and mathematical calculations to enable fully autonomous flight through residential and campus environments. To complement the delivery platform, we built an AI-driven health consultant using n8n that analyzes orders and provides guidance tailored to individual fitness and wellness goals. We also integrated Solana to demonstrate a fast, practical payment system that gives students an alternative to closed campus currencies while highlighting the real-world utility of blockchain. None of this would have been possible without an incredible team. Huge thanks to Utkarsh Banka and Mitansh Mittal —together, we took a bold idea and made it real under intense time constraints. An unforgettable 36-hour sprint and an even better learning experience 🚀 #CruzHacks #MajorLeagueHacking #MLH #Blockchain #Solana ...more

2025 was a transitional year that saw a lot of progress. It was a year of closing a chapter at Dougherty Valley High School and opening a new one at Santa Clara University. The journey of going through college acceptances and finally accepting Santa Clara was a major influence on the second half of the year. Having attended school on a semester system for four years, it took some adjustment to the quicker academic schedule of the quarter system at Santa Clara. Even in my first quarter, there were opportunities to get involved on campus and take on responsibilities. During the summer, I was chosen to participate in the SCU Ciocca Center Mindset Scholars Program, which offered an early move-in before the regular school year. The program focuses on mindset principles related to entrepreneurship, leadership training, and access to the resources offered at Santa Clara. Additionally, as part of this program, I was able to meet with Julie Sullivan, the President of Santa Clara University. Besides academics, being involved in campus life has also been a major point of emphasis. I have joined a number of student organizations, where I have been chosen and sworn in as a Santa Clara University Associated Student Government Representative for the Parking & Transportation Advisory Committee, as well as a Finance Office Manager for SCU ASG. The Santa Clara University Associated Student Government is a critical component of student voice and partnership with campus administrators, and serving in that capacity has meant a significant amount of responsibility. As I close 2025, the first quarter at Santa Clara University represents a strong start marked by adaptation, involvement, and responsibility that I am grateful for. Moving forward, I will continue to focus on learning, contributing, and developing on campus. ...more

my picture just went to space. literally. it was not edited onto a stock image. my photo was transmitted to SAT GUS, displayed on a Google Pixel 8 Pro aboard the satellite, and photographed with the actual Earth in the background. an idea that sounds impossible becomes real when enough talented people work together to build it. Mark Rober imagined the experience. CrunchLabs spent years turning it into reality. Tyvak, a Terran Orbital Company designed and built the SAT GUS satellite. Redwire Space, Inc. (Formerly Made In Space, Inc.) provided the specialized Argus camera used to capture the photo. SCHOTT provided the radiation-resistant glass protecting the camera system. SEOPS supported the satellite’s integration into the mission. Google Pixel provided the Pixel 8 Pro used to display each submitted picture. T-Mobile helped support and bring the project to millions of people. and on January 14, 2025, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carried SAT GUS into orbit aboard the Transporter-12 mission. now a full year later, I have an actual picture from space. moments like this remind me that engineering is not only about machines, calculations, or technology. it is about turning curiosity into something real. something that can inspire people. something that can make space feel a little closer to all of us. Huge credit to Mark Rober , CrunchLabs , SpaceX , Tyvak, a Terran Orbital Company International, Redwire Space, Inc. (Formerly Made In Space, Inc.) , SCHOTT , SEOPS , Google Pixel, T-Mobile , and every engineer and team member who contributed to SAT GUS. this might be the coolest picture I will ever receive. 🌎🛰️
